items.title: The site, now in three languages
items.body: The website now reads in English, Spanish, and French, each language at its own address. Every page is translated, along with the card and map-tile catalogues and the printable rulebook and player booklet. The words come straight from the game, so a card or a place reads the same on the site as it does at the table.

items.title: The print documents, refactored
items.body: The rulebook and player booklet were rebuilt from source in a typesetting pipeline, so they stay editable, reproducible, and true to the game's typography: a single illustrated reading manual, and a write-in booklet to print and fold.

items.title: A guest lecture in GRSJ 306
items.body: JOURNEYWAYS was brought into UBC's GRSJ 306 as a guest lecture, sharing the game and its approach to identity, play, and pedagogy with students.

items.title: A table that shows its hands
items.body: The shared table now feels alive. When you pick a card or tile it rides with your cursor until you set it down, and everyone watches it move, named to whoever is holding it, since nothing here is secret. Tiles can rest on top of one another in neat little piles with a small count, and moving the top one reveals the tile beneath. Along the bottom of the screen a quiet line tells the room what is happening: who is placing a card, moving a tile, or writing in their journal (never what they wrote). Open it and the line unfolds into a history with terse timestamps.

items.title: A new engine under the table
items.body: The game now runs on PostgreSQL. The shared table, every journal, and each session's state are stored as rich, nested objects, and PostgreSQL works with that kind of structured data natively, so the game saves and restores a session more quickly and holds it more reliably. Nothing changes in how you play; the engine just rests on sturdier ground.

items.title: A table to play on
items.body: The cards and map tiles now sit on a shared table. Everything is shuffled into uneven, face-down piles, each showing its suit on the back and the tiles on their wooden backs. Pick the top of a pile and it turns face up for the whole room to see, then place it wherever it belongs. An organizer can choose how many Countdown cards are in play and reshuffle the deck during a session, with everyone asked to agree first.

items.title: One catalogue, drawn once
items.body: Every card and tile is now drawn from a single shared definition, so the catalogue on this site, your dashboard, and the live game table all show exactly the same components. Each one scales cleanly to whatever size it needs while keeping its true proportions: a card stays a poker card, a tile stays a post-it square, and the art and text shrink and grow together.

items.title: Cards and map tiles, online
items.body: The full deck and the modular map now have a live catalogue you can browse on the site: every card sorted by suit, and every map tile, including the blank tiles you fill in yourself. Each set comes from the game itself, so the website always shows what is actually in play. See the cards and the map tiles.

items.title: Researchers, invitations, and scheduled rooms
items.body: Research rooms grow up. The person who creates one is its researcher, and can name others as researchers too, with a small tag beside each name. A researcher can configure a short set of optional questions (an age range, gender identity in your own words, a country) that you can skip; once anyone answers, they lock. Room creators can also invite people by email and open a room on a schedule.

items.title: Research rooms and open play
items.body: When you create a room you now choose whether it is for research or for open play. Joining a research room shows a short, plain-language screen explaining that the content you create there may be quoted, always anonymised, in the project's research, and joining is how you agree to that. Open play rooms stay private to the people in them.

items.title: Policy versions, recorded consent
items.body: Terms of Service and Privacy Policy now show their version and effective date at the top. When we update them in a way that changes what you agreed to, the next time you sign in you'll see a short re-acceptance screen with links to the updated text. Each acceptance is recorded against your account.

items.title: Live multiplayer presence
items.body: The "online" badge next to each room on your dashboard now updates in real time as players come and go, no page refresh needed. The lobby chips and the in-room presence pill also got a tighter visual pass with a "you" marker so it is clear which traveller is yours.

items.title: Right to forget your account
items.body: A new Danger zone on your profile lets you delete your account yourself, with a 30-day grace window so you can change your mind. Four reminder emails arrive over the month, each with a one-click cancel link. If you created rooms where other players have written journals, the action is blocked until you handle those rooms first, so collaborators don't lose work. Available in English, French, and Spanish.

items.title: Privacy audit pass
items.body: Stopped logging usernames at signup, removed an unused third-party analytics entry from the Content Security Policy, and verified the live deployment matches the privacy policy. Behind-the-scenes work.

items.title: Security and reliability audit
items.body: Closed several account-enumeration and brute-force vectors, made email verification and password reset race-safe, and cut admin-page query times via new indexes and query rewrites. Mostly behind-the-scenes work.

items.title: Password reset works
items.body: The "forgot password?" email now lands on a working form. Set a new password and sign back in.

items.title: Brand-aligned visual refresh
items.body: The videogame UI now follows the canonical palette (gray-900 base, yellow-400 accent), self-hosts Inter and Italianno, and uses script titles on atmospheric page headers. High-contrast checkboxes and toggles, with green and red reserved for semantic states.

items.title: A master's scholarship
items.body: The research behind JOURNEYWAYS was awarded a Canada Graduate Scholarship at the master's level (CGS-M) from the Social Sciences and Humanities Research Council, a national merit-based award supporting the project through its next phase at UBC GRSJ.

items.title: Multiplayer presence
items.body: Lobby, JOURNEY view, and dashboard now show who is in the room and who is currently playing.

items.title: Journal log redesign
items.body: Per-entry name, compact edit affordance, sketch preview thumbnails on each row.

items.title: A critical play fellowship
items.body: JOURNEYWAYS received the Critical Play Fellows Award, a UBC graduate award recognising the project's use of play as a mode of critical inquiry.

items.title: Play-view layout overhaul
items.body: Site navigation moved into a hamburger inside the journal panel. The canvas now reaches the top of the viewport. The journal panel can be hidden entirely or floated as an overlay.

items.title: Phone-size advisory
items.body: First-time-per-session modal warns phone users that the game is best on desktop or tablet. Full mobile responsiveness is on the roadmap.

items.title: mtime-based cache invalidation
items.body: Stylesheet and script tags carry an mtime-based version query so rebuilds invalidate browser caches automatically.

items.title: A guest lecture in EPSE 503
items.body: JOURNEYWAYS was brought into UBC's EPSE 503 as a guest lecture, sharing the game and its approach to identity, play, and learning with students.

items.title: Development begins
items.body: First commits on the digital companion to the boardgame.

items.title: Version 1.0, and a second playtest
items.body: The complete first edition came together: 35 map tiles, 81 cards across five colour-coded piles, the rulebook, and a write-in player booklet for each player. The game was played with the EDGES research group at UBC, an academic research-group session that fed straight back into the design.

items.title: First public playtest
items.body: JOURNEYWAYS took part in ProtoCON BC in Vancouver, a convention for playtesting game prototypes, and met its first table of players. Watching people pick cards, place tiles, and bend the loose rules to their own ends is where the game learns the most.

items.title: A Faculty of Arts award
items.body: The project received a Faculty of Arts Graduate Award from UBC, early institutional support for the research that became JOURNEYWAYS.

items.title: Design begins
items.body: General design of JOURNEYWAYS began: a loose-ruled game about identity and becoming, and the first shape of its map tiles, its five colour-coded card piles, and the write-in player booklet.
